plan.chapterName: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 4: Motion in Two and Three Dimensions
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a compact three-dimensional vector diagram drawn on a set of coordinate axes. The z-axis rises vertically, the y-axis extends to the right, and the x-axis runs toward the lower left, out of the page; all three are thin black lines with small arrowheads and italic labels, meeting at an unlabeled origin. Two purple dots mark positions in space, P_1 sitting above and to the right of the origin and P_2 lower and farther to the right. A thick purple arrow from the origin to P_1 is labeled r(t_1) and a second purple arrow from the origin to P_2 is labeled r(t_2), both symbols carrying overhead vector arrows. A third purple arrow of the same weight runs directly from P_1 to P_2 and is labeled delta r. The three arrows close into a triangle, so the picture shows the displacement as exactly the vector that must be added to the earlier position vector to arrive at the later one. Casting the difference of two position vectors as a single arrow drawn between the two points extends the one-dimensional idea of displacement to motion anywhere in space.

elements: x-axis: thin black line from origin toward lower-left (out of page) with arrowhead and italic label 'x'
y-axis: thin black line from origin to the right with arrowhead and italic label 'y'
z-axis: thin black line from origin straight up with arrowhead and italic label 'z'
unlabeled origin where the three axes meet
purple dot marking position P_1 (above and right of origin) with label 'P_1'
purple dot marking position P_2 (lower and farther right) with label 'P_2'
thick purple arrow from origin to P_1 labeled with vector r(t_1)
thick purple arrow from origin to P_2 labeled with vector r(t_2)
thick purple arrow from P_1 to P_2 labeled with vector Δr
closed triangle formed by the three arrows showing r(t_1) + Δr = r(t_2)

interactions.teaches: Moving P_1 or P_2 in 3D space redraws r(t_1), r(t_2) and Δr instantly while the triangle stays closed, making Δr = r(t_2) − r(t_1) visible as the single arrow that bridges the two positions no matter where they sit

interactions.label: Build the displacement
interactions.teaches: Stepping through origin→P_1, then origin→P_2, then P_1→P_2 reveals each vector in order, so the displacement is understood as exactly the change needed to carry the earlier position vector onto the later one

demo_steps.title: First position vector
demo_steps.narration: Only r(t_1) is drawn, an arrow from the origin to P_1. This is the particle's location at the earlier time.

demo_steps.title: Second position vector
demo_steps.narration: r(t_2) appears from the origin to P_2. Two position vectors now share the origin but point to different locations.

demo_steps.title: Displacement closes the triangle
demo_steps.narration: Δr is drawn straight from P_1 to P_2, closing the triangle. It is the vector that must be added to r(t_1) to reach r(t_2): Δr = r(t_2) − r(t_1).

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World axes span about ±3 units; standard isometric pose with +Y up, +X to lower-left (out of page), +Z to the right-ish per source tilt. Origin at (0,0,0). P_1 ≈ (0.6, 1.6, 1.1) and P_2 ≈ (1.4, 2.1, -0.4) in (x,y,z) world units so P_1 reads above-right and P_2 lower-farther-right of the origin as in the source; Δr = P_2 − P_1. Axes: thin black Line with small cone arrowheads, labels italic black. Position/displacement arrows: thick purple (#8e24aa) cylinders+cone heads, same weight. Dots P_1,P_2 purple spheres ~0.07 radius with black labels. Vector labels r(t_1), r(t_2), Δr in purple near each arrow midpoint. Triangle closure must hold exactly: head of r(t_1) + Δr lands on head of r(t_2).
interactionPlan.notes: Render each vector as a group (shaft cylinder + cone head) so its start/end can be re-aimed when a point is dragged; recompute Δr = P2 − P1 every frame. The drag interaction raycasts onto an invisible plane facing the camera through the dragged point so motion feels 3D. The button/state interaction only toggles visibility of the three arrow groups (show/hide, not rebuild) so the progressive reveal is cheap and the drag geometry is preserved across states. Keep labels as screen-space sprites or billboards so they stay legible from the isometric pose.

authoredContext:
With our definition of the position of a particle in three-dimensional space, we can formulate the three-dimensional displacement. The figure shows a particle at time t1 located at P1 with position vector r→(t1). At a later time t2, the particle is located at P2 with position vector r→(t2). The displacement vector Δr→ is found by subtracting r→(t1) from r→(t2):

Vector addition is discussed in Vectors. Note that this is the same operation we did in one dimension, but now the vectors are in three-dimensional space.

The displacement Δr→=r→(t2)−r→(t1) is the vector from P1 to P2.

An x y z coordinate system is shown, with positive x out of the page, positive y to the right, and positive z up. Two points, P 1 and P 2 are shown. The vector r of t 1 from the origin to P 1 and the vector r of t 2 from the origin to P 2 are shown as purple arrows. The vector delta r is shown as a purple arrow whose tail is at P 1 and head at P 2.

The following examples illustrate the concept of displacement in multiple dimensions.
